channel.title: horowitz.law: Georgia Legislative Watch
channel.description: Georgia legislation that became law (signed, or allowed to become law without signature) or was vetoed, read for a civil-litigation and insurance-defense practice. Each summary is AI-drafted and human-confirmed; the enrolled bill is the authority.

item.title: HB1247 — Georgia Bureaucratic Deference Elimination Act; enact (Enacted)
item.description: Part I of the Act, the Georgia Bureaucratic Deference Elimination Act, adds O.C.G.A. § 15-1-24, which bars a court, or an officer hearing an administrative action, from deferring to a state agency's written or unwritten determination or interpretation when interpreting Georgia's Constitution, statutes, or published rules, while leaving intact any standard of judicial review expressly established by statute. Previously, Georgia courts and hearing officers could give weight to an agency's construction of the laws it administers and of its own rules; parallel amendments to the Tax Court and Department of Revenue appeal and refund provisions (O.C.G.A. §§ 15-5B-16, 48-2-18, 48-2-35, 48-2-59) now require questions of law to be decided without deference to the Department, except for the deference accorded rules promulgated under the Administrative Procedure Act. Other parts of the Act make settlements of employment-practice claims against members of the General Assembly subject to redacted public disclosure, lower to a majority the legislative vote needed to override or block certain agency rules, and require five-year agency rule reviews beginning July 1, 2028; the Act took effect on the Governor's approval. Why it matters: Agency readings of statutes and rules no longer get deference in Georgia courts or administrative hearings unless a statute sets the review standard, opening regulatory interpretations to challenge. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1247/2025

item.title: HB1161 — Motor vehicles; proper operation upon approach by an authorized emergency vehicle or by a law enforcement vehicle for purposes of a traffic stop; provide (Enacted)
item.description: The Act amends O.C.G.A. § 40-6-74 so that the duty to pull to the right-hand edge of the roadway and stop extends to an approaching law enforcement vehicle using audible and visual signals, and adds a subsection governing a driver directed to stop by a marked law enforcement vehicle: the driver must move right without impeding traffic and stop until otherwise directed, but may signal, keep to the posted limit, and continue to a reasonably safe location when stopping would be unsafe. Georgia's existing rule addressed yielding to authorized emergency vehicles displaying audible and visual signals; because these are statutory rules of the road, violations supply a negligence per se theory in motor vehicle cases and a comparative-fault argument against a plaintiff driver. The Act also lowers the minimum light transmission for tinted front side windows and the rear windshield from 32 to 28 percent, sets fleeing-or-eluding sentences at 30 days per mile for pursuits by certain Department of Public Safety divisions, and revises school-zone speed camera permitting, revenue reporting, and citation notices; it took effect July 1, 2026, except the camera signage change, effective July 1, 2027. Why it matters: Revises Title 40 driver duties on the approach of emergency and law enforcement vehicles, usable as negligence per se or comparative fault in auto cases, and loosens front-window tint limits. Effective 2026-07-01. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1161/2025

item.title: HB295 — Local government; procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation for loss of property value or expenses incurred; provisions (Enacted)
item.description: HB295 amends Chapter 60 of Title 36 (general provisions for counties and municipalities) to create a statutory procedure by which real property owners may present claims to a local government for lost property value or expenses caused by that government's failure to comply with or enforce specified laws, ordinances, and resolutions, or by the local government's maintenance of a public nuisance. Previously, such claims against counties and cities proceeded under general tort, nuisance, and inverse condemnation theories subject to sovereign and official immunity defenses and generally applicable ante litem notice rules, with no dedicated compensation-claim mechanism in Chapter 60. The provided title and description do not specify the claim filing deadlines, notice content, response obligations, damages measures or caps, or whether and when suit may follow an unpaid claim, so those details must be confirmed from the enrolled text. Why it matters: Creates a new administrative claim path against Georgia local governments for property-value losses from nonenforcement or public nuisance, adding a pre-suit step to counsel. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB295/2025

item.title: HB1215 — Middle Judicial Circuit; superior courts; provide for a third judge (Enacted)
item.description: This act amends O.C.G.A. § 15-6-2, which sets the number of superior court judges by circuit, to add five superior court judgeships: a 21st judge in the Atlanta Judicial Circuit, a sixth in the Clayton Judicial Circuit, a third in the Middle Judicial Circuit, a sixth in the Northeastern Judicial Circuit, and a twelfth in the Gwinnett Judicial Circuit. Each new judge is appointed by the Governor (for the Atlanta, Clayton, and Middle seats, subject to appropriations) for a term running from January 1, 2027, through December 31, 2028, with successors elected at the 2028 nonpartisan judicial election to four-year terms. The act also authorizes an additional court reporter for each circuit, lets each circuit's judges divide the work and set the calendars, provides for electing the chief judges of the Middle and Gwinnett circuits, authorizes the counties to furnish courtrooms, facilities, and personnel, and declares the courts' inherent authority; it took effect on approval for purposes of the appointments and takes full effect January 1, 2027. Why it matters: Adds five superior court judgeships in the Atlanta, Clayton, Middle, Northeastern, and Gwinnett circuits from January 2027, changing judge assignment and calendaring for civil cases filed there. Effective 2027-01-01. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1215/2025

item.title: HB1187 — Trey's Law; enact (Enacted)
item.description: Enacted as "Trey's Law," this act fills reserved O.C.G.A. § 9-11-63 to make void and unenforceable, as against Georgia public policy, any nondisclosure or confidentiality provision of an employment agreement, settlement agreement, or other agreement to the extent it bars a person, including a party, from disclosing an act of childhood sexual abuse (as defined in O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33.1) or facts related to it. Previously, confidentiality and nondisclosure terms in settlements of such claims were generally enforceable as ordinary contract provisions; the act reaches agreements entered into before, on, or after its effective date, still lets parties keep other settlement terms such as the amount and payment terms confidential, and bars enforcing a covered provision without a final, unappealable declaratory judgment that it is enforceable. Although the act's title refers to confidentiality of victims' identifying information, the enacted text contains no separate provision on that subject; the act took effect on the Governor's approval. Why it matters: Nondisclosure terms can no longer bar disclosure of childhood sexual abuse or related facts, even in existing settlements, though settlement amounts and payment terms may still be kept confidential. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1187/2025

item.title: HB1185 — Courts; certain shareholder claims to be brought before the Georgia State-wide Business Court; provide (Enacted)
item.description: Amends Titles 14 and 15 to define an "internal entity claim" (O.C.G.A. § 14-1-1), covering derivative, fiduciary-duty, disclosure, valuation, and records-inspection claims involving corporations, LLCs, and partnerships, and lets a corporation's articles of incorporation or bylaws require such claims to be brought exclusively in the Georgia State-wide Business Court. Previously a defendant could object and force a case filed in the Business Court back to superior or state court; the Act bars that for internal entity claims where a governing document selects the Business Court or the entity is a public company, a Regulation A Tier 2 or Regulation D issuer, or an accredited-investor entity, adds a removal path for those claims, extends the window for agreed removal from 60 days to one year and for a petition to transfer based on the initial pleading from 60 to 90 days (with 15 days to object); a petition based on a later amended pleading keeps the 60-day window and 30-day objection period. The Act also lets listed corporations and limited partnerships set a derivative-standing ownership threshold of up to 1 percent, bars fee awards for disclosure-only derivative results, excludes pending or anticipated litigation from a "proper purpose" for records inspection, revises fee-shifting in inspection proceedings, and applies to claims initiated on or after July 1, 2026. Why it matters: Corporate, LLC, and partnership governance disputes can be locked into the Business Court by charter or bylaw, and derivative plaintiffs face ownership thresholds and no fees for disclosure-only results. Effective 2026-07-01. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1185/2025

item.title: HB1138 — Increasing Access to Contraceptives Act; enact (Enacted)
item.description: The Increasing Access to Contraceptives Act adds O.C.G.A. § 26-4-53 to authorize a pharmacist employed by a licensed hospital or pharmacy, acting in good faith and with reasonable care and after completing an approved certificate program, to dispense self-administered contraceptives and administer injectable contraceptives without a patient-specific written order under a written joint protocol agreement that the Department of Public Health and the Georgia State Board of Pharmacy must issue to take effect January 1, 2027 — conduct that previously required a practitioner's prescription. It adds O.C.G.A. § 33-24-59.37, requiring health benefit policies that cover prescription contraceptives to cover a three-month supply on the first fill and a 12-month supply on each later fill and to reimburse protocol dispensing at no less than the rate paid to physician assistants and nurse practitioners, and adds parallel Medicaid minimums and reimbursement at O.C.G.A. § 49-4-159.5. A pharmacist who dispenses or administers in accordance with § 26-4-53 is not subject to criminal or civil liability; the Act takes effect January 1, 2027, and applies to insurance policies issued, delivered, or renewed on or after that date. Why it matters: Creates a new insurer contraceptive-supply and pharmacist-reimbursement mandate and a statutory civil immunity that pharmacists dispensing under the protocol may assert in liability claims. Effective 2027-01-01. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1138/2025

item.title: HB1086 — Preston Fant and Brant Chesney Firefighter Safety Act; enact (Enacted)
item.description: The Preston Fant and Brant Chesney Firefighter Safety Act adds O.C.G.A. § 25-2-13.1, requiring the owner of any commercial or industrial building, or any multiunit residential building of three or more units, that uses light-frame truss-type construction or engineered I-joists to post a sign or symbol approved by the Commissioner warning firefighters and other emergency responders of that construction. The Commissioner must adopt rules setting the sign's dimensions, color, and location and the time owners have to comply, and the Commissioner and state and local fire marshals may enforce the requirement, with noncompliant owners subject to civil penalties under O.C.G.A. § 25-2-37. Owners within the covered class now carry an affirmative marking obligation they did not have under prior Chapter 2 provisions. Why it matters: Creates a statutory posting duty for owners that plaintiffs may invoke as a negligence per se or notice theory in premises and fire-loss litigation. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1086/2025

item.title: HB986 — Motor vehicles; personal delivery devices; revise operation procedures and restrictions (Enacted)
item.description: The Act amends Part 2A of Article 13 of Chapter 6 of Title 40, the portion of the motor vehicle code governing electric personal assistive mobility devices and personal delivery devices, to revise the operation procedures and restrictions that apply to personal delivery devices. Previously, PDD operation on sidewalks, crosswalks, and roadways was governed by the operating requirements as previously enacted in that Part; those requirements are now revised, though the provided description does not state which specific procedures changed. Practitioners handling claims involving sidewalk delivery robots should pull the current text of Part 2A rather than relying on prior versions. Why it matters: Revised statutory operating rules for delivery robots reset the negligence per se and comparative-fault baseline in pedestrian and vehicle collision claims involving personal delivery devices. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB986/2025

item.title: HB945 — Banking and finance; holds on accounts of eligible adults for suspected financial exploitation; provide (Enacted)
item.description: The Act amends Title 7 (banking and finance) to authorize financial institutions to place temporary holds on accounts of eligible adults when financial exploitation is suspected, and sets procedures for placing and lifting those holds. On the litigation finance side, it adds cease and desist procedures aimed at persons providing litigation finance without registration, creates a path for judicial hearings to review Department decisions on litigation finance matters, and imposes disclosure obligations on registrants. It also drops the requirement that independent credit reports be obtained from a consumer reporting agency as defined in the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, adds definitions, and makes conforming changes. Why it matters: Counsel handling funded claims should track new disclosure duties, unregistered-funder cease and desist exposure, and the judicial review route for Department litigation finance decisions. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB945/2025

item.title: HB185 — Professions and businesses; repeal and reenact Chapter 11A, the Dietetics Practice Act (Enacted)
item.description: HB185 repeals and reenacts OCGA Title 43, Chapter 11A, the Dietetics Practice Act, and makes conforming cross-reference amendments in Titles 9 (civil practice), 31, 33 (insurance), 43, and 51 (torts). The description identifies the Title 9, 33, and 51 changes only as conforming cross-references, so the substantive civil-practice rules appear unchanged; the provided text does not identify which specific code sections (for example, the professional malpractice affidavit or expert competency provisions that enumerate licensed dietitians) are being renumbered or relabeled. Practitioners relying on statutory references to dietitians or the prior chapter should verify current section numbers and any changed licensure terminology in the reenacted chapter. Why it matters: Renumbered dietetics licensure references may alter citations in malpractice affidavit, expert competency, and insurance statutes without changing substantive civil rules. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB185/2025

item.title: HB1128 — State Board of Workers' Compensation; notice of eligibility for compensation to an injured employee to his or her legal guardian; provide (Enacted)
item.description: Amends O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-26 and 35-1-24 so that the State Board of Workers' Compensation and law enforcement agencies may give the required notice of potential eligibility for the Georgia State Indemnification Fund and the temporary disability compensation program to the injured employee or to his or her legal guardian; previously those notice duties ran only to the employee. It also adds O.C.G.A. § 45-9-86.1, which, notwithstanding the usual application deadline in § 45-9-86(d), let a public safety officer or legal guardian apply for indemnification for a total permanent disability caused by organic brain damage sustained in the line of duty on or before July 1, 2024, where the injury prevented a timely application, but only between July 1 and August 1, 2026. That window has closed, and the Code section stands repealed on July 1, 2030; the Act took effect July 1, 2026. Why it matters: Counsel for incapacitated first responders should confirm eligibility notice reached the guardian; the one-time indemnification window for pre-July 2024 brain injuries closed August 1, 2026. Effective 2026-07-01. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1128/2025

item.title: HB944 — Motor vehicles; federal regulations regarding safe operation of commercial motor carriers and commercial vehicles; update reference date (Enacted)
item.description: O.C.G.A. § 40-1-8 incorporates the federal motor carrier safety regulations and hazardous materials rules into Georgia law by reference as of a fixed date, and adopting them for intrastate carriers. This Act moves that reference date forward, so the federal rules as amended through the newer date now control, and it revises a definition used in the Code section. The provided description does not identify the new reference date or the definition revised. Why it matters: Trucking cases must be measured against the newly incorporated version of the federal safety regulations, which govern negligence per se and standard-of-care theories. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB944/2025

item.title: HB1208 — Civil practice; require depositions to be taken before certified court reporters (Enacted)
item.description: Amends O.C.G.A. §§ 9-11-28 and 9-11-30 to require that depositions taken in Georgia be taken before a certified court reporter, as defined in O.C.G.A. § 15-14-22 or as provided by the rules of the Board of Court Reporting, and that deposition testimony be recorded by such a reporter, with sound or sound-and-visual recording still permitted in addition. It replaces the prior requirement that testimony be recorded by stenographic means, shifting the statutory focus from the method of recording to the qualification of the officer before whom the deposition is taken. Depositions by telephone or other remote electronic means still require a stipulation or court order; the Act took effect July 1, 2026. Why it matters: Georgia depositions must now be taken before and recorded by a certified court reporter, replacing the prior requirement that they be stenographically recorded. Effective 2026-07-01. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB1208/2025

item.title: HB339 — Motor vehicles; exempt ride share drivers or ride share network services from definition of motor carrier (Enacted)
item.description: HB339 amends Georgia's motor carrier article (Title 40, Chapter 1, Article 3) to expressly exclude ride share drivers and ride share network services from the definition of "motor carrier," adds definitions, and revises the article's legislative findings. It also provides that ride share network services are not liable for the actions of ride share drivers in certain circumstances, and makes conforming changes elsewhere in the article. Because the motor carrier designation is the gateway to the regulatory and insurance-related obligations imposed by that article, drivers and network services operating under this exemption are no longer treated as motor carriers for those purposes. The bill text as described does not spell out which circumstances trigger the liability exemption or how it interacts with any other basis for holding a network service liable, so those limits must be read from the enacted language itself. Why it matters: Ride share drivers and networks fall outside motor carrier status, narrowing claims and insurer-joinder theories that depend on that designation. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB339/2025

item.title: HB816 — Greene County Public Facilities Authority Act; enact (Enacted)
item.description: This local act creates the Greene County Public Facilities Authority, an entity that did not previously exist, and sets out its membership, powers, purposes, and authority to issue revenue bonds. Of direct relevance to litigators, the act includes provisions on tort immunity for the authority and fixes the venue and jurisdiction of actions involving it, along with provisions on moneys received and trust funds and tax exemption. Counsel handling claims arising from facilities or projects in Greene County should confirm whether the authority is the correct defendant and how its immunity and venue provisions apply before filing. Why it matters: Adds a Greene County public authority defendant with statutory tort immunity and fixed venue and jurisdiction for actions against it. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB816/2025

item.title: HB625 — Fulton County; State Court; provide additional judge (Enacted)
item.description: This local Act amends the 1976 consolidation Act creating the State Court of Fulton County (as amended in 1994 and 2003) to add two judgeships to that court, increasing its bench to twelve judges. The two additional judges are to be appointed by the Governor as soon as practicable after the Act's effective date, for terms beginning on the date of appointment and expiring December 31, 2026, and until successors are elected and qualified; thereafter the seats are filled by election. The additional judges have the same powers and privileges as the other judges of the court, and provision is made for compensation and expenses. Why it matters: Fulton County State Court gains two judges, bringing its bench to twelve and adding civil trial capacity in a high-volume venue for tort and insurance-defense cases. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB625/2025

item.title: HB114 — Motor vehicles; federal regulations regarding safe operation of commercial motor vehicle and carriers; update reference date (Enacted)
item.description: HB114 amends O.C.G.A. § 40-1-8 to update the reference date for incorporating federal safety regulations governing motor carriers, commercial motor vehicles, drivers, and hazardous-materials transport, and revises a definition within that section. The effect is to align Georgia's adopted federal safety standards with a more current version of the federal regulations. The bill text does not specify the new reference date or which definition is revised. Why it matters: Updated federal safety standards now apply as the negligence-per-se benchmark in commercial motor vehicle and trucking cases. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB114/2025

item.title: HB94 — Insurance; medically necessary expenses for standard fertility preservation services when a medically necessary treatment for cancer, sickle cell disease, or lupus may directly or indirectly cause an impairment of fertility; require coverage (Enacted)
item.description: Amends Chapter 24 of Title 33 to require certain insurance policies to cover medically necessary expenses for standard fertility preservation services when a medically necessary treatment for cancer, sickle cell disease, or lupus may directly or indirectly impair fertility. The Act provides definitions, exclusions, permissible cost-sharing, and authorizes implementing rules and regulations. The prior rule did not mandate this specific coverage; the text does not spell out the full scope of affected policies here. Why it matters: Expands mandated insurance coverage, potentially generating coverage disputes over fertility-preservation benefits tied to cancer, sickle cell, or lupus treatment. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB94/2025

item.title: HB179 — Appellate practice; digital recording of certain trial proceedings; provide (Enacted)
item.description: HB 179 amends the appellate practice provisions of O.C.G.A. Title 5, Chapter 6, Article 2, along with Title 9, Article 2 of Chapter 14 (post-conviction procedure) and Title 15 (courts, including the Georgia State-wide Business Court), to authorize digital recording of specified trial proceedings and to set rules governing the use and regulation of digital recording systems, with accompanying definitions. Previously, the statutory framework for making the record in these proceedings did not expressly provide for digital recording as an authorized method; the Act now supplies that authorization and its parameters. The description does not identify which specific proceedings may be digitally recorded, what certification or transcription requirements apply, or how a digital recording is to be reduced to a transcript for the record on appeal, so those details must be read in the enacted text. Why it matters: Civil litigators may face digitally recorded proceedings, including in the Business Court, changing how the record and appellate transcript are created and verified. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB179/2025

item.title: HB268 — Education; safety, health, and well-being of students and school communities; provide (Enacted)
item.description: HB 268 amends Chapter 2 of Title 20 to create an Office of Safe Schools within GEMA/HS, to require technical assistance for local school systems in developing threat management team policies and procedures, and to establish a state-wide behavioral threat management operational process with accompanying definitions. It also amends O.C.G.A. 16-11-37 to criminalize threatening death or serious injury to persons who are or are likely to be at school, and amends Article 4 of Chapter 18 of Title 50 to exempt certain records from public inspection. The text supplied does not identify which specific records fall within the Open Records exemption, nor does it state any immunity provisions for schools or threat management team members. Why it matters: Creates statutory school threat-assessment duties relevant to negligent security claims while shielding some related records from Open Records requests. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the enrolled bill. https://legiscan.com/GA/bill/HB268/2025
